No. A permanent phasing in does not trigger "when this creature enters" (enters-the-battlefield) abilities, and phasing out doesn't trigger leaves-the-battlefield abilities either.

Phasing is a status, not a zone change: a phased-out permanent is still on the battlefield, but the game treats it as though it doesn't exist and isn't under its controller's control. When it phases in, its status simply changes back to "phased in" and the game treats it as existing again [702.26c], [110.5b]. Because the phasing event doesn't actually move the permanent between zones or change control, zone-change triggers — which include enters-the-battlefield and leaves-the-battlefield triggers [603.6a] — don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out [702.26d]. Effects that check a phased-in permanent's history also won't treat the phasing event as having caused it to enter or leave the battlefield [702.26d].

Similarly, an Aura or Equipment that phases in or out doesn't cause "becomes attached/unattached" triggers to fire [702.26j]. Counters and stickers stay on the permanent throughout [702.26d].

Note that phasing in normally happens as a turn-based action at the start of the active player's untap step, simultaneously with that player's phased-in permanents with phasing phasing out [502.1], [702.26a], [703.4a]. This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the rules provided is that a permanent that phased out under the control of a player who has since left the game phases in during the next untap step after that player's next turn would have begun, and phased-out permanents can leave the game or be exiled when their controller leaves [702.26n], [800.4a].

Deathtouch changes what counts as lethal for that purpose: any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is treated as lethal damage [702.2c], and any damage above 1 from a deathtouch source is excess damage [120.4a].

So a 6/6 with trample and deathtouch blocked by two 4/4s can assign 1 to each blocker and 4 to the defending player. Each blocker still dies, because a creature with toughness greater than 0 that has been dealt damage by a source with deathtouch is destroyed as a state-based action [702.2b], [704.5h]. Note you must still assign at least 1 to each blocker; if you don't assign lethal (here, 1) to every blocker, you can't assign any damage to the player or planeswalker [702.19b]. If all blockers have left combat by the time damage is assigned, all the damage goes to the defending player/planeswalker as though lethal damage had been assigned to them [702.19d].

Terms: 'lethal damage' normally means damage greater than or equal to the creature's toughness, counting damage already marked on it and damage being assigned by other creatures in the same combat damage step [Lethal Damage], [702.19b]. Deathtouch overrides that threshold down to 1 for assignment purposes [702.2c].

One timing note: if the blocker already had damage marked on it, that doesn't matter here — 1 is enough either way with deathtouch. Ordinary trample without deathtouch would let you assign less because of the pre-marked damage [702.19b].

This all works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the only multiplayer wrinkle is which opponent is the defending player, and the provided rules don't add any special multiplayer assignment rules.

- If a spell somehow has multiple instances of storm, each one triggers separately, so each is a separate ability that would have to be countered separately [702.40b].

This works the same way in two-player and multiplayer games; nothing in the storm rules or the ability-countering rule depends on the number of players.

Layers are the game's ordering system for applying continuous effects to determine an object's current characteristics. You start with the actual object — for a card, its printed characteristics; for a token or a copy of a spell/card, the characteristics defined by the effect that created it — and then apply every applicable continuous effect in a fixed sequence of layers [613.1]. The game does this continually and automatically, and all resulting changes are instantaneous [613.5].

The layers named in the provided rules are:
- Layer 1: rules and effects that modify copiable values [613.1a]. Layer 1 has sublayers, starting with layer 1a, copy effects and merge-with-permanent changes; "as . . . enters"/"as . . . is turned face up" abilities generate copiable effects if they set power and toughness [613.2a]. After all of layer 1 is applied, the object's characteristics are its copiable values [613.2c], which is what a copy effect picks up [707.2].
- Layers 2–6 include control-changing (layer 2), type-changing (layer 4), color-changing (layer 5), and layer 6, ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects saying an object can't have an ability [613.1f], [613.6].
- Layer 7 (power/toughness) is broken into sublayers [613.4]; layer 7b sets power and/or toughness to a specific number or value, and layer 7c applies effects and counters that modify power/toughness without setting them [613.4c], [613.5].

Ordering within a layer: in layers 2–6, characteristic-defining abilities apply first, then all other effects in timestamp order [613.3], [604.3]; within each layer 1 sublayer and each layer 7 sublayer, effects apply in timestamp order [613.2], [613.4]. An earlier timestamp applies before a later one [613.7]. Dependency can override timestamp order: an effect depends on another if they're in the same layer/sublayer, applying the other would change the first effect's text, existence, what it applies to, or what it does, and neither (or both) come from characteristic-defining abilities [613.8], [613.8a]. Effects can also simply override one another, in which case the later timestamp "wins" [613.9].

One effect can split across layers: "gets +1/+1 and becomes the color of your choice" applies its color part in layer 5 and its +1/+1 part in layer 7c, and once it starts applying to a set of objects it keeps applying to them in each later layer even if its source is removed [613.6].

A +1/+1 counter (layer 7c) makes it 3/3; "+4/+4 until end of turn" (7c) makes it 7/7; "Creatures you control get +0/+2" (7c) makes it 7/9; then "becomes 0/1 until end of turn" applies in layer 7b — earlier than all of those — so the result is 0/1 plus +4/+4, +0/+2, and +1/+1, i.e. 5/8 [613.5], [613.4c].

Effects that affect players rather than objects (like giving a player protection from red) aren't in the layer system; they're applied in timestamp order after objects' characteristics are determined [613.10].

During the cleanup step — the second and final step of the ending phase — three things happen, in order:

1. Discard to hand size: if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to get down to that number. This is a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [514.1] [703.4n].

2. Damage removal and end-of-turn effects: immediately after that discard, simultaneously all damage marked on permanents (including phased-out permanents) is removed and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end. Also a turn-based action, not using the stack [514.2] [703.4p].

The exception: the game checks for state-based actions and for triggered abilities waiting to go on the stack (including abilities that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step"). If any exist, the state-based actions are performed, the triggered abilities are put on the stack, and then the active player gets priority and players may cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins, and the process repeats [514.3a] [704.3] [608.1].

If nothing needed doing on that first check, no player gets priority and the step simply ends as soon as its actions are complete [704.3] [500.3]. As the step ends, effects lasting until end of that step expire and any unspent mana in players' mana pools empties [500.5] [703.4q].

State-based actions are checked every time a player would receive priority — and they're handled before that player actually gets it.

How the check works: when a player would get priority, the game first looks for any of the listed state-based action conditions and performs all applicable ones simultaneously as a single event [704.3], [117.5]. If any were performed, the check repeats; if none were performed, any triggered abilities waiting to be put on the stack are put on the stack, and then the check repeats again. - Cleanup step: the same check process occurs, but if the step's first check performs no state-based actions and no triggered abilities are waiting, no player gets priority and the step ends [704.3], [514.3a]. If something is found, the state-based actions are performed, triggered abilities go on the stack, and the active player does get priority [514.3a]. The active player is simply the player whose turn it is; every other player is a nonactive player [102.1]. So you identify the active player by looking at whose turn is currently being taken — there's no other test needed.

A few clarifications that follow from that:

- Combat: during the combat phase the active player is the attacking player. In a two-player game the nonactive player is the defending player [506.2]. entries.answer:
A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by an effect that instructs a player to do something later in the game rather than right when the effect is created. [Delayed Triggered Ability] [610.2]

Key points from the rules:

- Wording: it contains "when," "whenever," or "at," though that word usually isn't the first word of the ability (e.g. "Exile this creature at the beginning of the next end step"). [603.7] [603.7c] Compare a normal triggered ability, written "[When/Whenever/At] [trigger event], [effect]" [603.1].
- How it's created: during the resolution of a spell or ability, as the result of a replacement effect being applied, or as a result of a static ability that lets a player take an action. [603.7a] A permanent spell with a static ability that functions on the stack creates its delayed triggered ability as the permanent enters the battlefield. [608.3g]
- It won't trigger until it has actually been created, even if the trigger event just happened; and earlier events can make the trigger event impossible (a "when this creature leaves the battlefield" delayed ability never triggers if the creature already left before the creating spell resolved). [603.7a]
- Duration: it triggers only once, the next time its trigger event occurs, unless it states a duration like "this turn." If the event happens more than once simultaneously with no stated duration, its controller picks which occurrence triggers it. [603.7b]
- Objects it tracks: it still affects a referenced object even if that object changes characteristics, but not if the object has left the expected zone (or left and returned, making it a new object). [603.7c] [400.7]
- Source and controller: if a spell created it, the spell is the source and the spell's controller as it resolved is the controller [603.7d]; if an activated or triggered ability created it, that ability's source and controller apply [603.7e]; for replacement effects or static-ability actions, the object with the static ability is the source [603.7f] [603.7g]. This is one of the exceptions to the usual controller rules. [109.4b] [108.4]
- Stack use: effects themselves don't use the stack, but delayed triggered abilities do go on the stack when they trigger. [405.6a]
- Special cases: an ability may create a delayed triggered ability that triggers when the creating ability has resolved a certain number of times in a turn; that delayed ability is created only once [603.7h]. If it refers to X without defining it, X equals the X chosen for the spell or ability that created it. [107.3n]

Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Most of an instant's or sorcery's text is a spell ability: an ability followed as instructions while that instant or sorcery spell is resolving. Any text on an instant or sorcery is a spell ability unless it's an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability meeting the criteria of rule 113.6 [113.3a] [Spell Ability].

So non-permanent spells can also carry the other categories of abilities:

In general, abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that object is on the stack (as opposed to abilities of other objects, which usually function only on the battlefield), with exceptions such as those in 604.6 [113.6]. entries.answer:
Everything that player owns leaves the game immediately, and the leftover objects they merely controlled get exiled. In order, per rule 800.4a: (1) all objects owned by that player (see rule 109.1 — cards, copies, tokens, spells, abilities on the stack, permanents, emblems) leave the game, and any effects giving that player control of objects or players end; (2) then any objects the departing player controlled on the stack that aren't represented by cards (e.g. their triggered/activated abilities, copies of spells) cease to exist; (3) then any objects still controlled by that player — ones owned by someone else, such as a creature stolen with Bribery — are exiled. This is not a state-based action; it happens the instant the player leaves, without using the stack (405.6h). If that player had priority, priority passes to the next player in turn order still in the game.

Details and exceptions:
• Objects owned by the departing player in the ante zone do not leave the game (800.4n; ante is an optional variant, 407.1).
• Phased-out permanents owned by the departing player also leave the game, and this does not trigger zone-change abilities (702.26k). A phased-out permanent that phased out under the control of a player who left phases in during the next untap step after that player's next turn would have begun (702.26n).
• A phased-in permanent leaving the game because its owner left the game does count as "leaves the battlefield," so leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger (603.6c, 603.10, Leaves the Battlefield).
• Nothing new can arrive under the departed player: objects don't change control to them, tokens for them aren't created, objects that would enter the battlefield or stack under their control stay put, and they can't control a player (800.4b). Objects they would own aren't created in any zone, and triggered abilities they'd control aren't put on the stack (800.4d).
• If a control-changing effect later ends and the default controller has left the game, the object is exiled at that moment (800.4c).
• Costs that a departed player would pay or choose to pay simply aren't paid (800.4f). Durations lasting until that player's next turn last until that turn would have begun (800.4m). If they left during their own turn, the turn finishes with no active player (800.4j).
• Planechase: face-up plane/phenomenon cards owned by the departing player leave the game and the planar controller turns up the next card; abilities from phenomena are an exception and stay on the stack under the new planar controller (901.10, 901.10b). Grand Melee has its own handling (901.14b).

This all applies specifically to multiplayer games (three or more players); in a two-player game a player leaving simply ends the game, so these rules never come up (800.4).

If any objects on the stack that aren't represented by cards were controlled by that player, those cease to exist; anything else that player still controlled at that point is exiled instead. None of this is a state-based action -- it happens immediately as soon as the player leaves.

If instead the ability belongs to a permanent controlled by a player still in the game (for example, another player's "Whenever another creature leaves the battlefield..." permanent), that ability does go on the stack and resolves normally — subject to range-of-influence restrictions in variants that use them: the trigger event must happen entirely within the range of influence of the ability's source's controller [801.7a].

entries.answer:
Activating a mana ability does not cost you priority — if you had priority before activating it, you still have priority immediately after it resolves, and you can act again right away.

Why: a mana ability is an activated or triggered ability that produces mana and follows special rules [113.4], [605.1]. It doesn't go on the stack, so it can't be targeted, countered, or responded to; it resolves immediately upon activation [605.3b]. Because nothing goes on the stack, no player gets a chance to respond, and rule [405.6c] states explicitly that if a player had priority before a mana ability was activated, that player gets priority after it resolves. Contrast casting a spell: the spell goes on the stack and, after casting, the caster retains priority only under the normal priority rules and the spell can be responded to before it resolves.

Two related points:
- You don't even need priority to activate a mana ability. You may do so whenever you have priority, whenever you're casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment, or whenever a rule or effect asks for a mana payment — even mid-cast or mid-resolution [605.3a], [117.1d], [608.2g]. For example, if declaring attackers requires a mana cost, the active player gets a chance to activate mana abilities then [508.1i]. Note that while a spell or ability is resolving, no player actually has priority, even though mana abilities may be activated [117.2e].
- A mana ability already begun can't be activated again until it has resolved [605.3c], and activating mana abilities is never mandatory [118.3c]. Any unspent mana sits in your mana pool and must be announced if you pass priority [106.4b], [117.3d].

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games; the only multiplayer wrinkle is that when you do eventually pass, priority goes to the next player in turn order [117.3d].
entries.answer_gold: It doesn't cost them anything -- activating a mana ability is one of the actions covered by the general priority rule that gives a player priority right back after they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action. Since a mana ability also never uses the stack and resolves immediately, its activator ends up right back with priority afterward, free to pass or do something else, rather than the turn simply moving on to the next player.

By contrast, a two-player game is one that *begins* with only two players ([100.1a]). The core rules apply to any game of two or more players either way ([100.1]).

- The game keeps going as players leave, rather than ending as soon as one player is gone ([800.4], [104.5]).

A game that began with four players stays a multiplayer game even after it's down to its last two combatants -- for example, its starting player would still not skip their first-turn draw step under the two-player rule, since that rule only applies to games that began with exactly two players.

entries.answer:
It's guaranteed, not a matter of choice: the nonactive player's copy of the ability resolves first, and the active player's copy resolves last.

Why: once abilities have triggered, they aren't put on the stack immediately — they wait until a player would next receive priority, and then they're put on the stack in APNAP (Active Player, Nonactive Player) order [603.3b]. APNAP order means the active player (the player whose turn it is) acts first, then each nonactive player in turn order [101.4]. Because the active player puts their triggered ability on the stack first, it ends up lower on the stack; the nonactive player's ability goes on top of it [603.3b], [405.3]. The stack resolves top-down as players pass priority, so the last thing put on resolves first [608.1]. Hence the nonactive player's instance resolves before the active player's.

Where choice does enter: a player who controls more than one triggered ability chooses the relative order of their own abilities among themselves [603.3b], [405.3]. But that never lets a player leapfrog another player's ability — the APNAP layering is fixed. Also note the two-part process in [603.3b]: abilities whose trigger condition is not "another ability triggering" go on the stack first (in APNAP order), then the remaining ones (in APNAP order). If your two identical abilities are both in the same part, the APNAP result above holds; if one of them triggers off another ability triggering, it goes on in the second pass and would therefore be higher on the stack and resolve earlier.

Multiplayer: the same rule scales. With more than two players, the active player's ability is lowest, then each nonactive player's in turn order (usually starting with the player to the active player's left), so the ability of the last nonactive player in turn order resolves first and the active player's resolves last [101.4], [603.3b], [405.3]. In two-player games this simply means the nonactive player's instance resolves first. (In the Two-Headed Giant variant the same idea applies at the team level: the active team places all its triggered abilities in any order, then each nonactive team does [805.7].)

One assumption: I'm reading "the same shared event" as both abilities triggering simultaneously off one event, before any player has received priority since. That's the case [603.3b] governs. If instead one triggered strictly later — after a player had already received priority and the earlier ability was already on the stack — then the later ability is put on top and resolves first regardless of who controls it. Note also that the order in which the abilities actually triggered is irrelevant to stack order [508.2b], [509.2a], [510.3a], [503.1a].
entries.answer_gold: It's guaranteed, not a free choice between the two players. APNAP order fixes it: the active player's copy of the trigger is placed on the stack first (ending up underneath), and each nonactive player's copy goes on afterward (ending up on top). Since the stack resolves top-down, a nonactive player's version of a shared trigger always resolves before the active player's version does, regardless of what either player would prefer.

The spell cast in response resolves first — the later-cast spell resolves before the spell that was already on the stack. 

Why: the stack tracks the order objects were added to it, and each new object goes on top of everything already there [405.2]. Casting a spell puts it on the stack [601.2i], so a spell cast while another spell is already on the stack is "in response to" that earlier spell, and it will resolve first [117.7]. Resolution happens one object at a time: each time all players pass priority in succession, the top (last-added) object on the stack resolves [608.1] [405.5]. "Resolves" means the object's instructions are carried out and it has its effect [Resolve] [609.1].

So the earlier spell just sits on the stack and waits; it resolves only after the responding spell has finished resolving (and after players pass priority again — the active player receives priority after each spell or ability resolves [117.3b]), and only if it's still legal and on the stack.

This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games: the stack is a shared, last-in-first-out zone regardless of player count, and players pass priority in turn order. (The one exception in the provided rules is the Grand Melee variant, which uses multiple stacks, one per turn marker; there a spell must be assigned to a specific stack, and it resolves first with respect to other objects on that same stack [807.5b].)

The stack always resolves its top (most recently added) object first once all players pass in succession.

A separate permanent that becomes a copy starts fresh — it can activate the ability that turn, even though the original permanent has already used up its "activate only once each turn" for the turn.

Why: the restriction is tracked per object, not per ability text. Rule 602.5b says a use restriction like "Activate only once each turn" continues to apply to that object (even if its controller changes) — i.e., it's the individual permanent that is "used up." Rule 602.5c adds that a restriction attached to an activated ability acquired from another object applies only to that acquired ability and not to other, identically worded abilities. So the copy's version of the ability is its own instance, with its own once-per-turn allowance.

Copying also doesn't carry over the fact that the ability was used. Rule 707.2a says a copy acquires only the copiable values — those derived from printed text (name, mana cost, color indicator, types, rules text, power/toughness/loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, face-down status, and "as . . . enters" abilities that set P/T; other effects, status, counters, and stickers are not copied. "I already activated this ability this turn" is game history about a particular object, not a copiable characteristic, so the new copy has no such history.

Timing assumption: I'm reading the question as one permanent activating its ability, and then a *different* object (a clone-style permanent, whether it entered as a copy per rule 707.5 or was turned into a copy by a later copy effect) becoming a copy of it. Under that reading, the new copy may activate once that turn. If instead you mean the very same permanent that already activated is merely given new copiable text (it's still the same object), then rule 602.5b keeps the restriction on that object and it cannot activate again this turn.

Related note: rule 700.10 says a permanent "that was activated this turn" means that permanent was the source of an ability activated this turn — again object-by-object, so the fresh copy wasn't "activated this turn" just because the thing it copies was.

A "once each turn" restriction is tracked per object, and it does keep following an object even if that object's controller changes -- but a copy created by a copy effect is a brand-new object with no memory of its previous existence, so it isn't the same object that already used the ability and hasn't used its own copy of that restricted ability yet this turn.
